title: Planning a presentation on urban gardens
lines: So, Maya and Josh, how is the presentation on urban gardens coming along?
Quite well, I think. We've decided to focus on community gardens rather than private ones, because there's more research on them.
And it's more relevant to our course, which is about public planning.
Good. What sources have you found?
The most useful has been a report by the city council. It has lots of figures on how many gardens there are and who uses them.
Although some of the figures are quite old. They're from about ten years ago.
That's worth mentioning in the presentation. Anything else?
There's a journal article by a researcher called Hendricks. She interviewed gardeners about why they took part.
I thought that was the most interesting part, actually. Most people said the main reason wasn't the food. It was meeting their neighbours.
That's a common finding. How are you dividing up the work?
I'll do the history and the figures, and Maya will talk about the social benefits.
And we were going to finish with a case study. We visited the garden on Elm Street last week.
Excellent. What did you notice there?
The biggest problem they have is water. There's no tap on site, so they carry it from the houses nearby.
They also said it's hard to get young people involved. Most of the gardeners are retired.
Those are both good points to raise. Now, the presentation is twenty minutes. Have you timed it?
Not yet. I think we've got too much material, to be honest.
Then I'd cut the history section down. The examiners are more interested in your analysis than in background.
That makes sense. Should we use slides?
Yes, but keep the text short. Photographs from your visit would work well.

title: Feedback on a business report
lines: Come in, Lena. I've read your report on the coffee shop chain. Overall, it's a good piece of work.
Thank you. I wasn't sure about the structure.
The structure's fine. Your introduction is clear, and the conclusion follows from your findings. Where I think you could improve is the analysis of the competitors.
It's not the length. You describe what the competitors do, but you don't say what that means for the company. You need to compare.
I see. So, for example, the competitor that opened near the station: I should say how that affected sales?
Exactly. Now, your survey. How many customers did you ask?
That's a reasonable number for a project like this, but you need to explain how you chose them. Otherwise the reader can't judge whether the results are reliable.
I just asked people as they left the shop.
That's fine, but say so, and mention that it might mean you missed people who use the drive-through.

I liked the idea of a loyalty app. That's realistic and you've costed it well. The idea of opening in the evening is less convincing, because your own survey shows very few people want coffee after six.
That's true. I suppose I could suggest selling food in the evening instead.
You could, but you'd need evidence for it. And one small thing: your graphs need titles and labels on the axes.
Oh, I forgot those. When do you need the final version?
By Friday the twelfth. Email it to me, please, rather than handing in a paper copy.

title: Choosing a research method
lines: So we need to decide how to collect data for the sleep project. I was thinking of an online questionnaire.
That's the easiest, but I'm worried people won't remember how long they slept. They'll just guess.
True. What about sleep diaries? People write down the times every morning for two weeks.
That's more accurate, but lots of people give up after a few days. Dr Grant said that happened in her study.
We could send a reminder by text each morning.
That might help. And if we offered a small reward at the end, like a voucher, more people might finish.
Our budget is tiny, though. Fifty pounds at most.
Then maybe a prize draw. One person wins the whole fifty.
Good idea. Now, who should we ask? Just students?
If it's only students, the results won't apply to anyone else. But it's realistic for a three-month project.
Let's do students, then, and say clearly in the report that it's a limitation.
Agreed. And we need ethical approval before we start. The form goes to the department committee.
About three weeks, I think, so we should submit it this week.
I'll start filling it in tonight. Can you design the diary?
Sure. I'll keep it to one page, so it's quick to fill in.

title: A field trip to the coast
lines: Let's talk about the field trip to the coast next month. Have you both read the information sheet?
Yes. We're studying coastal erosion at three sites, right?
That's right. At the first site, the cliffs at Redcliff, you'll measure how far the cliff edge has moved since our last visit.
There are metal posts at fixed points. You measure from each post to the edge with a tape.
And the second site is the beach at Sandbay?
Yes. There you'll collect pebbles at different points along the beach and measure their size. The idea is to see how the waves sort them.
That's the harbour, where a sea wall was built in the nineteen nineties. You'll interview local people about whether they think it has worked.
Interviews? I thought this was a physical geography trip.
It mostly is, but managing the coast affects people, so it's important to hear their views.

Waterproof clothing, definitely, and strong shoes, because the rocks are slippery. We'll provide the measuring equipment. And bring a packed lunch for the first day, as there are no shops near the cliffs.
Will we be working in groups?
In groups of four. I'll put you in groups so that each one has someone who can drive, as you'll need to get between the sites.
Two thousand words, due three weeks after the trip. Most of the marks are for your discussion of the data, not the description of the sites.

title: Comparing two textbooks
lines: We have to recommend one of these two textbooks for next year's first-years. Which did you prefer?
Honestly, I liked Introduction to Psychology by Marsh better. The explanations are much clearer.
I agree it's easier to read, but it's six years old. Some of the research it describes has been questioned since.
That's a fair point. The Cooper book is more up to date.
And it has those online quizzes for every chapter. Students like that kind of thing.
Do they work, though? When I tried them, half the links were broken.
Oh, I didn't check. That would be a problem.
There's also the price. Cooper is nearly twice as expensive.
The library could buy more copies, maybe. Then cost wouldn't matter so much.
Maybe. What did you think of the case studies?
Marsh's are better. They're real examples, and they make you think. Cooper's are invented and a bit obvious.
So Marsh wins on clarity and case studies, and Cooper on being current.
Could we recommend Marsh, but tell students which chapters are out of date?
That works. Let's add a short list of recent articles to read alongside it.
Good. I'll write that list if you write the summary for the course leader.

title: Group project on plastic waste
lines: Right, the three of you are working on reducing plastic waste on campus. Where have you got to?
We did a survey of the bins in the main canteen for a week. Most of the plastic was drinks bottles.
Followed by sandwich packaging. Cups were less of a problem than we expected, because the canteen already uses paper ones.
Interesting. And what are you going to recommend?
Water fountains. There are only two on the whole campus at the moment.
We'd like the university to install at least ten more, and to sell cheap refillable bottles in the shop.
Have you looked at the cost?
Yes. Each fountain costs about eight hundred pounds to install. We think the money saved on cleaning and bins would cover it in a few years.
You'll need figures to support that. Who could give you them?
The estates office. We've emailed them but haven't heard back.
I'd go in person. They're very busy, and emails get lost. What about the sandwich packaging?
That's harder. The supplier says cardboard packaging would cost more and the sandwiches wouldn't stay fresh as long.
Then perhaps present it as an area for further research rather than a firm recommendation.
Good idea. And we're planning a short video to show at the student union.
Just make sure you get permission from anyone who appears in it.

title: Preparing for a work placement
lines: So, Tom, your placement at the engineering firm starts in September. How are you feeling about it?
Excited, but a bit nervous. I've never worked in an office before.
That's normal. Have you been in touch with your supervisor there?
Yes, she emailed me a list of things to read, mostly about the company's safety procedures.
Good. Make sure you read those before you start. Now, the university also needs some things from you. You have to keep a weekly log of what you've done.
Does that count towards my mark?
Not directly, but your final report is based on it, so it's worth keeping it properly. Most students who struggle with the report didn't keep a log.
You choose one project you worked on and reflect on what you learned. It's three thousand words.
And will someone from the university visit me?
Yes, once, about halfway through. It's mostly to check that you're getting useful work and not just making coffee.
My friend said his placement was very boring.
If that happens, tell me early. We can talk to the company. But do ask for work yourself, too; supervisors appreciate students who show initiative.
Ask your supervisor. Engineering offices are often quite casual, but you might need safety boots for site visits.

title: Analysing survey results on reading habits
lines: So, the results are in. Two hundred people answered our survey about reading habits.
The first surprise for me was that more people read on paper than on screens. I expected the opposite.
Me too. Although the younger group did read more on phones, mostly news rather than books.
And the most common reason for not reading more was lack of time. Nearly half said that.
Cost came much lower down. Most people use the library or borrow books from friends.
How should we present this? A pie chart for the reasons?
A bar chart would be clearer, because people could choose more than one reason, so the percentages don't add up to a hundred.
Good point. And for paper versus screen, a simple table by age group?
Yes. I think we should also mention the weaknesses of our survey. We only advertised it online.
Which means we probably missed people who don't use the internet much, and they might read more on paper.
Exactly. It could even mean the paper figure is too low.
Let's put that in the limitations section. When's our next meeting with the supervisor?
Thursday at two. I'll bring the draft charts.
